seo.metaTitle: Light Pixel Mask - Mark Bright Areas Of An Image
seo.metaDescription: Select the pixels brighter than a luminance threshold and see them as a mask. Free and local: the image is analyzed in your browser, never uploaded.
seo.longDescription: Light pixel mask marks every pixel above a luminance threshold — the weighted mix of red, green and blue that matches how the eye perceives light. Use it to pull out highlights, check whether a photo is overexposed, or separate the light part of an image from the rest to work on it separately. The threshold is a percentage of full brightness, and the default is set high so only genuinely bright pixels appear. Everything runs in your browser, so the image is never uploaded.
facts: Runs entirely in your browser: no upload, no server, no signup.
Marks pixels above a luminance threshold; threshold 100 is pure white only.
Two views: a black and white mask, or a highlight over the original picture.
Luminance weights match human perception — green counts most, blue least.
Free with no daily limit, no watermark and no account, also for commercial use.
howTo: Drop the image into the source area, or pick a file from your device.
Choose the view: a black and white mask, or a highlight over the original picture.
Move the luminance threshold: higher values mark only the brightest pixels.
Set the highlight color and opacity, then download the mask.

faq.a: By luminance, which combines the red, green and blue values with weights that match human perception: green contributes most, blue least. That is why a pure yellow pixel reads brighter than a pure blue one of the same channel values.
It is the brightness level a pixel has to reach, as a percentage, to be marked. A threshold of 100 marks only fully white pixels, a low value marks most of a bright image.

faq.q: What can I use the mask for?
faq.a: Finding blown-out highlights before you compress an image, isolating the bright part of a photo, or checking how much of a design sits above a brightness level - for example to test text contrast.
No. The image is decoded and the mask is rendered in your browser tab; the file is never sent to a server and nothing is stored.
